# Overview

### Bias Is the Default

### Disrupting the "Computer Science Degree" Myth:

### Understanding the Need for Diversity

### Building Multicultural Capacity

Exceptional engineers need more than technical skill. They also need the
perception to understand how a product can advantage one group while
disadvantaging another, and when a feature should be delayed or rejected
because its possible harms have not been addressed. This requires building
multicultural capacity: learning about the different communities affected by a
product, seeking perspectives beyond our own experiences, and continuing to
develop our understanding of race, gender, ability, age, culture, and
socioeconomic status.

This responsibility cannot fall on one person alone. Engineering teams should
include perspectives that reflect their current and future users, while
organizations should provide ongoing, multidisciplinary professional
development. When a team lacks representation, engineers can still improve
their work by researching the people most likely to be excluded, involving
community members and subject-matter experts, and testing the most difficult
use cases first. Designing with the users who face the greatest barriers often
creates a better experience for everyone.

### Making Diversity Actionable

Making diversity actionable means turning good intentions into measurable
responsibility. Leaders should examine whether candidate pools, hiring
decisions, opportunities for advancement, and retention outcomes are equitable
instead of assuming that a policy is effective because it has inclusive goals.
Teams should also measure product outcomes across different user groups and
investigate disparities when they appear. These steps make equity part of the
engineering process rather than an issue considered only after harm occurs.

Progress also depends on accountability. Managers can review whether candidate
slates are representative, distribute growth opportunities fairly, and create
psychological safety for people from underrepresented groups. Engineers can
question processes that rely on incomplete data or narrow definitions of a
successful user. Together, these actions help organizations move from building
for everyone in theory to building with everyone in practice.

### Rejecting Singular Approaches

One of the main statements that you as a software engineer should hold close is: "If we want to drive change and increase representation, we need to evaluate whether we’re creating an ecosystem in which all aspiring engineers and other technology professionals can thrive." We need to stay aware of the fact that the software engineering field is not a monolith, and that there are many different ways to approach problems. 

We need to be open to new ideas and perspectives, and we need to be willing to challenge our own assumptions. One common methodology is to build for the majority use case first, leaving improvements and features that address edge cases for later. This approach gives users who are not part of the majority use case a subpar experience, and it can be frustrating for them to have to wait for improvements that address their needs. We need to be willing to challenge this approach and to build for all users from the start.

### Challenging Established Processes

A case at Google was evaluated for equity implications. Multiple engineering teams got together to try to build a new feature, a global hiring requisition system. Their main line of communication was the feedback from what would be the main users of this new feature, recruiters. The recruiters main focus was to minimize wasted time when it comes to hiring. One of the main features they wanted added was the ability to highlight performance ratings as soon as interest was expressed in a job by an internal transfer. This raised some questions by another engineer:

- Are developmental assessments a predictive measure of performance?
- Are the performance assessments being presented to prospective managers free of individual bias?
- Are performance assessment scores standardized across organizations?

If you answered "no" to any of these questions, then this new feature could drive inequitable, and therefore potentially harmful, results. 

After seeing the potential for inequitable results, a study was conducted in which those with a lower performance rating were discovered to have a higher likelihood of overcoming the poor rating if they found a new team. These results showed that while ratings are important, they are only indicative of a person's performance at that moment in time, and that they are not a predictive measure of future performance.

### Values vs Outcomes

Despite a strong commitment, heavy investments, and inclusive core values, Google continuously misses its goal of building a hiring workforce that represents its global user base. The issue does not arise within company values or intentions, but rather in how policies are applied and practiced at the implementation level. Feedback is easy to gather when you rely on those familiar, but do not consider those that you may not have reached yet.

How can we ensure that our values are reflected in our outcomes? 

1. Take a hard look in the mirror. 
    - True inclusivity requires fixing implementation failures and breaking old habits, rather than relying solely on good intentions or company values.
2. Don’t build for everyone. Build with everyone.
    - To build universally accessible technology, products must be designed with diverse communities, highlighting the most vulnerable populations, rather than assuming their needs.
3. Design for the user who will have the most difficulty using your product.
    - Don’t trade equity for short-term velocity.
    - Prioritizing and solving for the users who face the greatest barriers automatically improves the overall product experience for everyone.
4. Don’t assume equity; measure equity throughout your systems.
    - Keep in mind that even those who make decisions can also be undereducated and subject others to bias. Companies must be sure to continuously measure equity across all systems and collaborate with teams and individuals who are subject matter experts to expose and mitigate implicit biases.
5. Change is possible.
    - Overcoming modern, overwhelming digital challenges requires a fundamental willingness to abandon outdated, failing approaches in favor of continuous self-change.
